title: The 'Made in India' Stamp That Ended Ardeshir Godrej's Scalpels
dek: A Bombay lawyer who would not bend the truth in court lost his first factory over a label, then began making locks in a shed in 1897.

story.event: Abandoning a surgical-instrument venture over a 'Made in India' label and starting to make locks in a Lalbaug shed
story.summary: After giving up law in 1894 rather than argue a claim he could not honestly prove, Ardeshir Godrej borrowed 3,000 rupees from family friend Merwanji Cama in 1895 to make surgical instruments; by the company's account the venture ended when he insisted they be stamped 'Made in India' and the proprietor refused. Prompted by reports of rising burglary in Bombay, he began making locks on 7 May 1897 in a small shed at Lalbaug, the start of Godrej & Boyce.
paragraphs: In 1894 Ardeshir Godrej, just out of law school in Bombay, was sent by a firm of solicitors to argue a case in Zanzibar. He refused to tell the court something he could not honestly prove, came home and gave up the law. "Instead of seeing my side of the case, I saw both sides, the plaintiff's as well as the defendant's," he said later. He found work as an assistant to a chemist in a pharmacy.

In 1895 he set out to make surgical instruments. He asked Merwanji Cama, a family friend respected for his business sense, for a loan. Why not ask your father, Cama wanted to know; Ardeshir answered that his father would make it a gift, and he wanted a loan. Cama lent him 3,000 rupees, and he began making scalpels, forceps and scissors. Then, by the account his company still tells, he insisted that the instruments be stamped "Made in India". The proprietor refused, apparently judging that Indian-made surgical instruments would not sell, and the venture ended. Godrej held, that history says, that India could win independence only through industry of its own.

He did not go back to the law. He read a newspaper report on rising burglary in Bombay and the police commissioner's call for better security, and turned to locks. On 7 May 1897, in a shed of about 20 square metres beside the Bombay Gas Works at Lalbaug, he started production with a dozen skilled workers from Gujarat and Malabar. His first were high-security locks under the Anchor name.

This time the work held. His Detector lock, which showed whether anyone had tampered with it, won a gold medal at the Calcutta Industrial and Art Exhibition of 1900. Safes followed from 1902, and his younger brother Pirojsha joined him in 1906. Within about a dozen years the brothers had patented a lock that worked without springs. A partnership with Cama's nephew, Boyce, gave the firm the name Godrej & Boyce, and the factory doubled in size and came to employ 600 people.

quote.text: it will be acknowledged, even by those that practise it not, that clear, and round dealing, is the honor of man's nature; and that mixture of falsehoods, is like alloy in coin of gold and silver, which may make the metal work the better, but it embaseth it.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon admits what the proprietor saw: a little falsehood can make the metal work better. Godrej refused the alloy twice, in a Zanzibar courtroom and over a stamp on a scalpel, and it cost him two beginnings before the third one held.

reflection: It is easy to read this as a story about patriotism, and it partly is. It is also about a young man who kept finding that he could not do a job the way it was offered to him, and who did not take that as proof he was unfit for work. He took it as information about which work was his.

You may have a version of the stamp: a small thing you are asked to say or sign that would make something run more smoothly, and that you know is not quite true. Refusing it can cost you a beginning. Godrej's story suggests that a beginning is something you can make again.
invitation: Name one small untruth that your work currently asks of you, even a convenient rounding or a label. Decide today whether you will keep it, change it, or raise it with someone.

cross_checks.claim: In 1894 Godrej gave up law after refusing to argue what he could not honestly support in a case in Zanzibar.
His surgical-instrument venture, funded by a loan from Merwanji Cama, failed.
The venture ended when he insisted on stamping the instruments 'Made in India' and the proprietor refused.
Lock production began in 1897 (7 May) in a small shed at Lalbaug, Bombay.
Pirojsha joined his brother and the brothers patented a springless lock.

research_notes: The 'Made in India' dispute is the heart of the episode but rests on the company's own history and Wikipedia (which draws on B. K. Karanjia's authorised biography Vijitatma, 2004); The Better India, also drawing on Karanjia, says only that the surgical-instrument business 'did not do well'. Search results also showed The Week (2023) reporting a variant in which a hospital asked for 'Made in England' to be printed on the instruments, but that page could not be read, so it is not cited. The story therefore attributes the stamp to 'the account his company still tells' and gives the proprietor's reasoning tentatively. Neither source names the proprietor. Purpose of Cama's loan: the company history and Wikipedia say the 3,000 rupees were lent for surgical instruments; The Better India says Godrej borrowed from Cama to start the lock business; Wikipedia also says the locks began 'with Cama's funding'. The story ties the loan only to the instruments and does not say how the lock shed was financed. Springless lock: the company history says a British patent in July 1908; Business Today dates the invention and patent to 1909; the story says 'within about a dozen years'. The company page also says Godrej 'employed forty steam presses' in the 20 m² shed; this is hard to reconcile with the shed's size and is omitted. Wikipedia's story that Cama later refused repayment is not used because no other source carries it. 'Bootstrapped' reflects a personal loan from a family friend rather than outside investment. The Business Standard article cited by Wikipedia (1998) returned 403 to the fetch tool and is not cited. Bacon's sentence concerns 'the truth of civil business'; it is applied by analogy to the label.
